intro: Searching for architects near me usually means you have a building project in mind and want someone local who can see the site and understand the area. You may be planning an extension, a conversion, a new build or alterations that need planning and building regulations drawings. We can introduce you to a suitable UK architecture practice, and they will quote you directly, price on application.
need_heading: What people searching for local architects usually need
need_lead: Most people looking for architects near me are at the start of a project and want to know who can help them turn an idea into drawings and approvals.
needs: You are planning a house extension or loft conversion and need drawings for planning permission and building regulations.
You have bought a property and want to remodel the layout, perhaps removing walls or reconfiguring the kitchen and living space.
You are considering a new build on a plot and need help with design, planning and the technical drawings that follow.
You need to alter a listed building or a property in a conservation area and want someone used to the extra approvals involved.
You want a local architect who can visit the site, talk through options and oversee the work through to construction.
context_heading: Knowing who you are really hiring
context: "Architect" is a protected title in the UK. Only people on the Architects Registration Board (ARB) register can call themselves architects, and they must follow the ARB code of conduct and hold professional indemnity insurance. Many practices are also RIBA Chartered Practices. Architectural designers and technologists can do excellent work too, but they are not registered architects, so it is worth knowing which you are hiring.

Before you appoint anyone, check the ARB register and ask for a written appointment that sets out services, fees and responsibilities. Building regulations approval, planning permission and party wall matters are separate processes that your architect can help you navigate.
tell_heading: What to tell us when you enquire
tell: Describe the property, including its type, age and whether it is listed or in a conservation area.
Explain what you want to achieve, such as an extension, a conversion, a new build or a change of layout.
Say whether you already have planning permission, building regulations approval or any drawings.
Mention your rough budget and whether it has been discussed with a lender or adviser.
Give your location so we can introduce you to a practice that works in your area.
Note any deadlines you are working towards, such as a planning application or a purchase completion.
questions: Are you on the ARB register, and is the practice a RIBA Chartered Practice?
What stages of work will you carry out, and how do these map to the RIBA stages?
Will you handle the planning application and building regulations submission, or is that separate?
How will you keep me informed of costs as the design develops?
What is included in your fee, and what might be charged separately?
Can you provide a written appointment setting out services, fees and responsibilities?

faqs.q: Do I need an architect for a house extension?
faqs.a: Not always, but an architect can prepare drawings for planning permission and building regulations and help you avoid problems later. Some alterations are permitted development, while others need a formal application, so it is worth checking before you start.

faqs.q: What is the difference between an architect and an architectural designer?
faqs.a: An architect is on the ARB register and must follow its code of conduct and hold professional indemnity insurance. Architectural designers and technologists are not registered architects, though they can do excellent work, so it is worth knowing which you are hiring.

faqs.q: How do I check someone is a registered architect?
faqs.a: You can check the ARB register before you appoint anyone. Ask for a written appointment that sets out services, fees and responsibilities, and confirm whether the practice is a RIBA Chartered Practice.

faqs.q: Can an architect help with planning permission and building regulations?
faqs.a: Yes, an architect can prepare drawings for planning and building regulations and can help you navigate those separate processes. Party wall matters are also separate, and your architect can advise on when they apply.

extra: Searching for architects near me in the plural suggests you are weighing up more than one practice rather than looking for a single name. That is a sensible approach for a building project, because practices differ in the kind of work they take on, how they charge and how they like to run a job. Comparing a few locally means you can judge which one suits your property and your plans.

When you speak to each practice, ask how they would approach your specific project and which RIBA stages they would cover. Ask what their fee covers and what is charged separately, such as planning submission, building regulations drawings or site visits during construction. It also helps to ask how many projects like yours they have handled locally, and whether they have worked with your local planning authority before.

Price is only part of the picture, so compare the scope behind each quote rather than the headline figure alone. A written appointment that sets out services, fees and responsibilities makes practices easier to compare fairly. Take your time over the decision, because the architect you appoint will shape your project from the first sketch through to completion.

extra_faqs.q: Should I meet more than one architect before deciding?
extra_faqs.a: Meeting a few practices is a good way to compare approaches, fees and how well you communicate with each other. Ask each one what they would do for your project and what their written appointment would cover.

extra_faqs.q: How do I compare quotes from different architects fairly?
extra_faqs.a: Look at what each quote includes rather than the total alone, since one may cover planning and building regulations drawings while another treats them as extra. Ask for the scope to be set out by RIBA stage so the comparison is like for like.

extra_faqs.q: Will a local architect know my area's planning authority?
extra_faqs.a: A practice that regularly works in your area will usually be familiar with the local planning authority and the kinds of applications it deals with. It is still worth asking directly about their experience with your type of property and project.
